Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I identified the factual basis by locating the statements that describe DHS’s policy, the directives and guidance, the named plaintiffs, and the court orders. I extracted verbatim snippets that directly support the summary of facts and used them as evidence.

evidence: Filed March 23, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, this certified class action challenges the Department of Homeland Security’s policy and practice of removing noncitizens with final removal orders to “third countries” (countries not designated on the removal order) without prior meaningful notice and an opportunity to seek protection from persecution or torture.
The factual core alleges DHS has no operative process to ensure notice and a pre‑removal hearing when it seeks to remove an individual to a third country.
On February 18, 2025, DHS directed officers to re‑detain previously released individuals for potential third‑country removals.

On March 30, 2025, DHS issued “Guidance Regarding Third Country Removals” allowing removal without any process where the United States has blanket diplomatic assurances from the receiving country, and otherwise providing only notice and rapid (often 24‑hour) screening if, without prompting, an individual affirmatively voices fear.

The named plaintiffs exemplify the allegations. A Cuban man (final order to Cuba) faced imminent re‑detention and third‑country removal; a Honduran woman with 2021 withholding to Honduras was told she was on a deportation list; an Ecuadorean man granted CAT protection in 2018 was re‑detained; and a Guatemalan man granted withholding to Guatemala in February 2025 was quickly deported by DHS to Mexico without notice or a chance to raise fear; Mexico then removed him to Guatemala, where he remains in hiding.
Judge Brian E. Murphy granted a TRO on March 28, 2025, enjoining third‑country removals without written notice and a meaningful opportunity to seek CAT protection.

On April 18, 2025, the court certified a class of individuals with final orders who DHS has removed or will remove on or after February 18, 2025, to a country not designated or identified in writing in their prior proceedings.
On May 20, 2025, DHS began removing eight class members to South Sudan with fewer than 24 hours’ notice.

Following emergency hearings, on May 21 the court found DHS violated the injunction, clarified that “meaningful opportunity” requires a minimum of 10 days after notice, and ordered remedial relief: DHS must provide private reasonable‑fear interviews, with 72 hours’ notice, counsel access (in‑person or remote) and interpreters, and post‑interview procedures (including a 15‑day period to seek reopening after a negative screening), either in the United States or abroad so long as DHS retains custody/control and ensures access equivalent to that provided in the U.S.

On May 23, 2025, the court ordered DHS to facilitate the immediate return to the United States of the named plaintiff who was removed to Mexico without notice after winning withholding to Guatemala, following DHS’s later admission that it could not identify any officer who had asked him about fear of Mexico as previously represented.
The First Circuit denied DHS’s request for a stay of the preliminary injunction (Order of Court, May 16, 2025).
On June 23, 2025, the Supreme Court stayed the district court’s preliminary injunction pending appeal and any petition for certiorari (DHS v. D.V.D., 145 S. Ct. 2153).

Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I identified the key factual elements by reviewing the summary, noting the dates, parties, executive actions, legal claims, court orders, compliance steps, and subsequent motions that form the factual basis of the case.

evidence: Filed on February 28, 2025, this class action in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts challenges a series of federal executive actions that (1) terminated humanitarian parole programs and (2) halted adjudication of immigration benefits for parolees.
Plaintiffs are individual parole beneficiaries (or would-be beneficiaries), U.S.-based sponsors (including military families), and Haitian Bridge Alliance.

Plaintiffs contend that, on Inauguration Day (January 20, 2025), the President issued Executive Orders directing DHS to terminate “categorical parole programs” (including the parole processes for nationals of Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela (collectively CHNV)), limit parole to case‑by‑case decisions, and re‑establish rigorous vetting.

Acting DHS Secretary Huffman then issued a memorandum authorizing pausing/terminating categorical parole programs; Acting CBP Commissioner Flores limited CBP parole authority; and Acting USCIS Director Higgins directed staff to cease decisions on parole, re‑parole, and other benefit applications for beneficiaries of programs such as Uniting for Ukraine (U4U), CHNV, Operation Allies Welcome (OAW), Family Reunification Parole (FRP), and Central American Minors (CAM).

On February 14, 2025, Acting USCIS Deputy Director Davidson ordered an 'administrative hold' on adjudicating immigration benefits (e.g., asylum, TPS, adjustment) for U4U, CHNV, and FRP parolees based on potential vetting deficiencies.

On March 25, 2025, DHS published a Federal Register Notice terminating the CHNV parole processes and providing that all unexpired CHNV paroles and associated employment authorization would end April 24, 2025, absent individualized contrary determinations.

Plaintiffs assert that these actions are contrary to the INA and the APA (5 U.S.C. §§ 701‑706) because they misinterpret the parole statute, impose categorical decisions where case‑by‑case determinations are required, and arbitrarily suspend adjudications. They also invoke the Accardi doctrine and allege Fifth Amendment Due Process violations.

On April 14, 2025, the court preliminarily stayed the March 25 CHNV notice insofar as it revoked existing CHNV grants of parole and work authorization without case‑by‑case review, and certified a class of individuals whose CHNV parole grants were being truncated.

The First Circuit denied a stay pending appeal on May 5, 2025, but on May 30, 2025, the Supreme Court stayed the district court’s April 14 order pending appeal and any petition for certiorari, allowing DHS’s mass truncation of CHNV parole to go forward (over a dissent).

On May 28, 2025, the district court granted partial preliminary relief on plaintiffs’ broader motion, staying: (1) the January 23 Higgins directive to the extent it suspended adjudications of re‑parole and other non‑parole benefits for parolees under the identified programs; (2) any DHS actions suspending initial parole/re‑parole and related benefits under Military Parole in Place (MPIP); and (3) the February 14 Davidson memorandum to the extent it suspended adjudications of immigration benefit applications for U4U, FRP, and CHNV parolees and required case‑by‑case lifting of the hold even in the face of classwide court orders.
The court then issued compliance orders requiring DHS/USCIS to resume adjudications, update system “holds,” contact‑center scripts, and public messaging, and to report on implementation.

USCIS issued the June 9 'Alfonso‑Royals' memo authorizing resumption of adjudications, and reported lifting system holds by June 19, 2025, with adjudicator guidance to follow; the court continues to monitor compliance, including issues raised by plaintiffs about lingering 'administrative hold' messaging and diversity‑visa processing for class members.

Defendants moved to dismiss on May 30, 2025, arguing lack of standing, jurisdictional bars under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B), nonfinal/nonreviewable agency action under the APA, and failure to state an APA or due process claim.

Plaintiffs also moved for partial summary judgment on June 16, 2025, seeking to vacate DHS’s mass truncation of CHNV parole; defendants opposed on July 7, 2025, and an amicus (Immigration Reform Law Institute) filed in opposition.
On August 1, 2025, the district court denied the remaining portion of plaintiffs’ earlier PI motion addressing suspensions of initial parole adjudications for persons outside the U.S.
Throughout the case, plaintiffs have proceeded under pseudonyms by court order, and several state and organizational amici have participated. No settlement has been reached.

evidence: Filed on February 13, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, this case challenges the creation and actions of the “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) established by executive order on January 20, 2025, and the role of Elon Musk as an unpaid special government employee.

The plaintiffs—originally 26 current and former personnel of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), later narrowed and re‑pleaded as six pseudonymous representatives—allege that, beginning in late January 2025, DOGE personnel directed by Musk rapidly assumed control over USAID’s systems and operations, closed USAID’s headquarters and disabled its website, placed large numbers of USAID employees on administrative leave, terminated or attempted to terminate thousands of grants and contracts, and initiated a reduction-in-force to wind down the agency.

The plaintiffs claim DOGE members without proper clearances accessed sensitive systems and data, and that these actions disrupted legally mandated programs and jeopardized safety and security of USAID personnel and beneficiaries.

The factual allegations underlying the claims include that DOGE teams—often including personnel with prior ties to Musk—were embedded across agencies; that on January 27, 2025 they began demanding and receiving administrator‑level access to USAID systems; that Musk and DOGE orchestrated the closure of USAID headquarters, took down the agency website, blocked staff access to systems, and removed signage; that large numbers of employees and contractors were placed on administrative leave or issued RIF or termination notices; and that mass terminations of grants and contracts were directed.

The case remains in the district court on the constitutional claims, with a partial injunctive relief framework initially issued by the district court but stayed by the Fourth Circuit; no trial has occurred, and there is no settlement.

The case was filed on February 13, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, the plaintiffs bring two constitutional claims: (1) violation of the Appointments Clause, alleging Musk exercised “significant authority” as the de facto DOGE leader without Senate confirmation or lawful statutory vesting; and (2) violation of the separation of powers, alleging that defendants’ actions to dismantle or abolish USAID—an agency established by law and funded by Congress—contravene Congress’s exclusive authority to create, fund, and abolish agencies.

On March 18, 2025, after expedited briefing and a hearing, Judge Chuang granted a preliminary injunction in part. The court found plaintiffs likely to succeed on both claims as to key actions: the court concluded Musk appeared to have made the decisions to permanently close USAID headquarters and take down USAID’s website without approval by a duly appointed USAID officer, and that the broader effort to “effectively eliminate” USAID was incompatible with Congress’s establishment and ongoing appropriations for the agency.

On March 28, 2025, a Fourth Circuit panel stayed the preliminary injunction pending appeal, concluding defendants made a strong showing of likely success and emphasizing, among other things, that many actions were taken or ratified by USAID officials and that plaintiffs had not sued the proper agency defendants at the time of the injunction.
extracted.value: The case involves the creation of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) by executive order on January 20, 2025, with Elon Musk serving as an unpaid special government employee. Plaintiffs, former and current USAID personnel (originally 26, later narrowed to six), allege that starting in late January 2025 DOGE personnel directed by Musk took control of USAID’s systems and operations, closed its headquarters, disabled its website, placed employees on administrative leave, terminated thousands of grants and contracts, and initiated a reduction‑in‑force to wind down the agency. They claim DOGE members accessed sensitive systems without proper clearances, disrupting legally mandated programs and jeopardizing safety and security of USAID staff and beneficiaries. Evidence supporting these allegations includes DOGE teams embedded across agencies, the demand for administrator‑level access to USAID systems on January 27 2025, the closure of headquarters, the takedown of the website, the blocking of staff access, the removal of signage, the placement of employees on administrative leave or receipt of RIF/termination notices, and the directed mass termination of grants and contracts. Background context includes the filing of the case on February 13 2025, the constitutional claims of violation of the Appointments Clause and separation of powers, the preliminary injunction granted by Judge Chuang on March 18 2025 (later stayed by the Fourth Circuit on March 28 2025), and the ongoing status of the case with no settlement.

The case challenges a January 20, 2025 Executive Order (No. 14169) directing an immediate “pause” in foreign development assistance and a January 24, 2025 State Department memorandum instructing an immediate suspension and issuance of stop‑work orders for existing foreign‑assistance awards.

The court granted in part a temporary restraining order on February 13, 2025, enjoining enforcement of the State memorandum and other directives implementing EO 14169 “including by” suspending or preventing disbursements, or issuing/maintaining stop‑work orders and terminations, for awards in existence as of January 19, 2025.

On March 10, 2025, the court granted in part a preliminary injunction, holding plaintiffs likely to succeed on their APA claim that the initial directives implementing the blanket “pause” were arbitrary and capricious, and it enjoined the government from giving effect to suspensions/terminations or withholding payments for work completed before February 13 on awards in existence as of January 19.

Factual context: Plaintiffs averred—and the district court credited at the TRO/PI stages—that EO 14169 and the January 24 State memorandum caused an immediate, across‑the‑board suspension of foreign‑assistance disbursements and stop‑work orders, disrupting global health, humanitarian, and democracy‑assistance programs, prompting widespread layoffs and shutdowns, and jeopardizing vulnerable populations.

Plaintiffs filed an amended complaint on May 2, 2025 (adding the Center for Victims of Torture) alleging that after the TRO the government mass‑terminated most awards (roughly 9,900 of about 13,100 in both agencies) based on cursory review and form letters, and asserting these later terminations are arbitrary and contrary to law (APA).

evidence: Filed on February 10, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington (Seattle), this case challenges actions taken by the federal government on and after January 20, 2025, related to the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP).

The plaintiffs are eight individual refugees or U.S.‑based family/sponsors, and three nonprofit organizations central to refugee resettlement—HIAS, Inc., Church World Service, Inc. (CWS), and Lutheran Community Services Northwest.

They sue the President, the Secretary of State (Marco Rubio), the Secretary of Homeland Security (Kristi Noem), and the Secretary of Health and Human Services (Dorothy A. Fink, later Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.) in their official capacities.

The suit challenges Executive Order 14163, “Realigning the United States Refugee Admissions Program,” issued January 20, 2025, which indefinitely suspended refugee entries under USRAP and suspended decisions on refugee applications pending future presidential determinations.

Plaintiffs also challenge how agencies implemented the order: the State Department canceled refugee travel before the order’s effective date, suspended all case processing, and on January 24, 2025, issued stop‑work notices and halted USRAP funding to resettlement partners under a separate foreign aid review order (EO 14169).

On February 26, 2025, the State Department terminated resettlement partners’ cooperative agreements for domestic reception and placement services and, for most, overseas processing support through Resettlement Support Centers.
Plaintiffs allege these steps dismantled USRAP infrastructure, stranded refugees who had been approved and booked to travel, and cut off statutory post‑arrival services to new arrivals.

The complaint pleads violations of the Immigration and Nationality Act/Refugee Act (8 U.S.C. §§ 1157, 1522), the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (arbitrary/capricious, contrary to law, failure to follow required procedures), the Accardi doctrine, separation‑of‑powers principles, and the Fifth Amendment due process rights of “follow‑to‑join” petitioners.
Plaintiffs seek declaratory and injunctive relief and class certification.

On February 25, 2025, Judge Jamal N. Whitehead granted a preliminary injunction (written order issued February 28) enjoining enforcement of EO 14163’s suspension provisions and enjoining the suspension of refugee processing, decisions, admissions, and USRAP funding (including withholding of pre‑January 20 reimbursements).

The court found plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits: the President’s order likely exceeded 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) because it effectively nullified Congress’s refugee scheme and lacked the required findings, and the agencies’ implementation and funding suspensions were likely arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law.
The court also found due process concerns for follow‑to‑join petitioners and issued a nationwide injunction.
On March 25, 2025, the Ninth Circuit stayed the injunction in large part, but denied a stay as to individuals conditionally approved for refugee status before January 20, 2025.

On April 21, 2025, the Ninth Circuit clarified that the carve‑out applied to those who, by January 20, had: (1) an approved refugee application authorizing conditional admission per 8 C.F.R. § 207.4; (2) USCIS travel clearance; and (3) arranged and confirmable travel plans.
On May 9, 2025, the court further clarified the carve‑out should be applied narrowly, case‑by‑case, to individuals with strong reliance interests comparable to the lead plaintiff.

Meanwhile, the district court allowed a supplemental complaint addressing the February 26 terminations and, on March 24, 2025, issued a second preliminary injunction enjoining the State Department’s termination of USRAP cooperative agreements and ordering reinstatement.

The court held APA jurisdiction, found the terminations likely contrary to the Refugee Act’s resettlement scheme (8 U.S.C. § 1522) and arbitrary and capricious, and denied the government’s request for a bond.

Initially (May 5), the court set detailed steps to resume processing for injunction‑protected refugees, but rescinded that framework (May 15) after the Ninth Circuit’s May 9 clarification requiring individualized reliance assessments.
On July 14, 2025, the court entered an “Injunction Implementation Framework” appointing Magistrate Judge Michelle L. Peterson to manage case‑by‑case reliance determinations.

The court defined “Review‑Eligible Cases” (those meeting the Ninth Circuit’s three criteria, including certain pre‑January 20 travel cancellations after December 1, 2024) and “Injunction‑Protected Refugees” (those with Pacito‑comparable reliance interests).

The framework created a rebuttable presumption of sufficient reliance for: (1) approximately 160 refugees with travel within two weeks of January 20, 2025; (2) unaccompanied minor children; and (3) certain Afghan refugees processed via Camp As Sayliyah.

It directed the government to identify Review‑Eligible Cases, notify applicants, facilitate standardized reliance surveys via RSCs, conduct initial decisions, and litigate disputed cases before Judge Peterson, whose reports and recommendations would be subject to objection and final ruling by Judge Whitehead.

Class certification was granted on July 30, 2025, under Rule 23(b)(2) for three subclasses: (1) Refugee and Family Member Subclass (represented by Pacito, Sara, Alyas, Marcos, Josephine, and Ahmed); (2) Reception & Placement Subclass (represented by Ali); and (3) Follow‑to‑Join Petitioner Subclass (represented by Esther).
IRAP and Perkins Coie were appointed class counsel. On the same date, the court denied the government’s motion to dismiss, rejecting jurisdictional and merits challenges.

Throughout, the Ninth Circuit issued stay and clarification orders narrowing the district court’s injunction to a case‑by‑case carve‑out, later issuing an administrative stay on July 19, 2025, pending resolution of an emergency motion concerning the implementation framework.

The litigation remains ongoing on appeal (Nos. 25‑1313 and 25‑1939) and in the district court under the implementation framework, with the preliminary injunctions in force as narrowed by the Ninth Circuit.

Judge Jamal N. Whitehead presides in the district court; Magistrate Judge Michelle L. Peterson oversees reliance determinations under the framework; and Judges Silverman, Bade, and De Alba comprise the Ninth Circuit panel.

evidence: On February 7, 2025, the States of Washington, Minnesota, and Oregon, together with three University of Washington pediatric physicians, filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington (Seattle) to challenge President Trump’s January 28, 2025 Executive Order 14,187, “Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation,” and, later by amendment, the January 20, 2025 Executive Order 14,168, “Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government.” Colorado joined as a plaintiff on February 19, 2025. Plaintiffs are represented by their respective state Attorneys General; the physicians are represented by the Washington Attorney General. Defendants are the President (official capacity), the United States, and multiple federal departments and agency heads, including HHS, DOJ, and others.

Plaintiffs bring constitutional claims under the Fifth Amendment’s equal protection component, the separation of powers, the Tenth Amendment, and (as to EO 14,168’s definitions of “sex,” “male,” and “female”) the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause (vagueness), invoking the Declaratory Judgment Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 2201–2202. They seek declaratory and injunctive relief. The challenged provisions are: (1) Section 4 of EO 14,187, which directs agency heads to “immediately” take steps to ensure institutions receiving federal research or education grants end gender‑affirming care for “children” (defined in that order as individuals under 19); (2) Section 8(a) of EO 14,187, which instructs the Attorney General to prioritize enforcement of 18 U.S.C. § 116 (female genital mutilation); and (3) Sections 3(e) and 3(g) of EO 14,168, which require agencies to end federal funding of “gender ideology” and ensure grant funds do not promote “gender ideology.”

Judge Lauren King granted a temporary restraining order on February 14, 2025, enjoining enforcement or implementation of Section 4 of EO 14,187 within the plaintiff states and enjoining Section 8(a) to the extent it purported to redefine “female genital mutilation” under 18 U.S.C. § 116 as the order’s “chemical and surgical mutilation.” In a February 16 memorandum, the Court found Plaintiffs likely to succeed on separation‑of‑powers grounds (improperly conditioning congressionally appropriated grants), equal protection (sex and transgender‑status discrimination), and the Tenth Amendment (intruding on state regulation of medicine by attempting to expand § 116), and found standing based on threatened loss of funds, forced policy choices, and credible enforcement risks.

After Plaintiffs amended the complaint to add Colorado, claims against EO 14,168’s funding instructions, and a vagueness claim, the Court held a preliminary‑injunction hearing on February 28, 2025. That day, the Court granted in part and denied in part Plaintiffs’ motion. The preliminary injunction (1) enjoined all Defendants (other than the President) from enforcing or implementing Section 4 of EO 14,187 within Washington, Oregon, Minnesota, and Colorado; and (2) enjoined enforcement of Sections 3(e) and 3(g) of EO 14,168 to condition or withhold federal funding based on the fact that a health‑care entity or professional provides gender‑affirming care within those four states. The Court denied preliminary relief as to Section 8(a) of EO 14,187 for lack of standing, finding no credible threat of prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 116 on the record presented.

Following the injunction, Plaintiffs moved for contempt, citing NIH’s February 28 termination of a Seattle Children’s Hospital research grant related to transgender youth and HHS/CDC notices referencing the executive orders. On March 17, 2025, the Court denied contempt but granted expedited discovery limited to whether the NIH termination contravened the preliminary injunction, and ordered Defendants to correct an “unreasonable” interpretation of the injunction—clarifying that “gender‑affirming care” is not confined to the four treatments listed in EO 14,187 and that research may involve patient care. Defendants provided notice of compliance on March 20. On March 27, 2025, NIH reinstated the Seattle Children’s grant in full, and the Court later denied as moot Plaintiffs’ motion to compel further discovery.

Defendants filed an interlocutory appeal to the Ninth Circuit (No. 25‑1922) from the preliminary‑injunction order (and the expedited‑discovery order) on March 21, 2025. On April 23, 2025, the District Court stayed further district‑court proceedings pending appeal, with important exceptions: the stay does not bar proceedings to enforce or clarify the preliminary injunction, motions to amend or seek additional preliminary relief (including on any new claims), or motions for relief from the stay. The Court noted similar limited‑stay terms entered in related litigation (PFLAG, Inc. v. Trump, D. Md.) and observed that the issues on appeal are largely legal (ripeness, Article II authority, level of scrutiny), and that Supreme Court review in Skrmetti is expected to provide guidance.

Throughout, the District Court documented a concrete factual basis: the Executive Orders sought to cut off federal research and education grants to medical institutions providing gender‑affirming care; agencies issued rapid notices referencing the orders; a White House press release stated the orders were “already having [their] intended effect”; and some hospitals curtailed care pending legal developments. Plaintiffs presented evidence of immediate harms to research funding and patient care at institutions such as the University of Washington School of Medicine, Oregon Health & Science University, Oregon State University, and Children’s Hospital Colorado, and described the medical‑community consensus that gender‑affirming care, when indicated, is the standard of care for adolescents with gender dysphoria.

Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I analyzed the case summary to identify the key facts, supporting evidence, and background context that constitute the factual basis of the case. I extracted the relevant sentences as evidence and synthesized them into a comprehensive summary.

evidence: On March 26, 2025, eleven nonprofit legal service organizations that represent unaccompanied immigrant children filed this APA action in the Northern District of California against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), its Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), and the Department of the Interior (DOI).

The organizations—based in California and across the country—alleged that the Government’s abrupt March 21, 2025 termination of contract line items for direct immigration representation of unaccompanied children violated the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 (TVPRA), 8 U.S.C. § 1232(c)(5), and ORR’s 2024 Unaccompanied Children Program Foundational Rule, 45 C.F.R. § 410.1309, and was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The suit arises from a long-running federal program under which ORR funds legal services for unaccompanied children—children under 18 without lawful status and without a parent or legal guardian available in the United States—to ensure, “to the greatest extent practicable,” they have counsel in legal proceedings.

On March 21, 2025, DOI issued a “Notice of Partial Termination for the Government’s Convenience” of Contract No. 140D0422C0009, canceling the line items for direct representation, attorney recruitment/IJC fellows, and language tutoring (CLINs 2–4), while leaving only know-your-rights presentations and consultations (CLIN 1).

Plaintiffs alleged that Congress has appropriated funds for TVPRA services—including direct representation—through September 2027 and that ORR’s Foundational Rule obligates ORR, subject to appropriations, to fund providers to deliver direct representation when pro bono counsel is not practicable.

Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted a temporary restraining order on April 1, 2025, enjoining Defendants from withdrawing ORR-provided services or funds as of March 20, 2025, particularly the provision of funds for direct legal representation, and precluding cutting off access to congressionally appropriated funding during the TRO.
The court later extended the TRO to April 30, 2025.

The Government moved to dissolve the TRO (arguing, inter alia, that the Tucker Act channeled the dispute to the Court of Federal Claims and that the Supreme Court’s April 4, 2025 decision in Department of Education v. California barred APA orders compelling payments), and also sought the judge’s recusal based on past employment at a plaintiff organization.
The court denied recusal on April 17, 2025 and denied dissolution of the TRO on April 21, 2025.

Plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction. After hearing on April 23, 2025, the court granted a preliminary injunction on April 29, 2025, preserving the status quo and prohibiting the Government from withdrawing the ORR funding and services for direct representation provided as of March 20, 2025.

The court found Plaintiffs likely to succeed on their APA claims that the termination contravened the TVPRA’s mandate to “ensure, to the greatest extent practicable” that unaccompanied children have counsel, and the Foundational Rule’s requirement that ORR fund direct representation (subject to available appropriations) where pro bono representation is not practicable.

The court also credited evidence of available appropriations for legal services through September 2027, and Plaintiffs’ declarations describing imminent layoffs, service cuts, and the risk that children would appear in immigration court without counsel.

On appeal, the Government’s challenge to the TRO was dismissed by the Ninth Circuit on April 18, 2025 for lack of jurisdiction; rehearing en banc was denied April 25, 2025, and the mandate issued May 5, 2025.

The Government noticed an appeal of the preliminary injunction on April 30, 2025 and moved for a stay pending appeal. On May 14, 2025, the Ninth Circuit (Judge Koh, with Judge Callahan dissenting) denied the stay, holding the Government had not shown a likelihood of success on its arguments that the Tucker Act impliedly barred APA review or that the termination decision was committed to agency discretion by law, and had not demonstrated irreparable injury absent a stay.

Throughout the case, amici curiae—including Former Immigration Judges and Former HHS Officials—supported Plaintiffs, addressing the importance of counsel for unaccompanied children and ORR’s historic provision of funded representation.

The district court’s preliminary injunction remains in effect, enjoining Defendants from cutting off ORR funding and services for direct legal representation of unaccompanied children during the pendency of the litigation.

Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I reviewed the case summary to identify the factual events, evidence, and background context that form the factual basis of the case. I extracted the key facts such as the filing date and parties, the abrupt mid‑February 2025 grant terminations and their justification, the internal directive, the complaint’s APA basis, the background teacher shortage and program reliance, the TRO and Supreme Court stay, the Department’s motion to dismiss or transfer, and the remedies sought.

evidence: On March 6, 2025, eight states (California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Colorado, Illinois, Maryland, New York, and Wisconsin), represented by their Attorneys General, filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts against the U.S. Department of Education, the Secretary of Education, and the former Acting Secretary (in their official capacities).

The states challenge the Department’s abrupt mid‑February 2025 termination of virtually all previously awarded grants under two federal teacher pipeline programs—the Teacher Quality Partnership (TQP) Program (authorized by the Higher Education Act, 20 U.S.C. § 1022 et seq.) and the Supporting Effective Educator Development (SEED) Program (authorized by the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, 20 U.S.C. § 6672).

The states allege the Department sent standardized termination letters to grantees, asserting the awards no longer effectuated Department “priorities,” including concerns about alleged DEI‑related discrimination, but without program‑specific reasons or individualized analysis.

The terminations followed a February 5, 2025 internal Department directive, issued amid new Executive Orders addressing “DEI,” directing staff to review grants for discriminatory practices and for consistency with Department policy objectives.

The complaint, brought under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. §§ 701–706, seeks declaratory and injunctive relief to vacate and set aside the terminations, alleging they are arbitrary and capricious, contrary to law, ultra vires, and inconsistent with notice‑and‑comment priority‑setting requirements in GEPA (20 U.S.C. § 1232(d)) and the Department’s regulations (34 C.F.R. § 75.105).

The states also invoke the OMB Uniform Guidance—particularly 2 C.F.R. § 200.340—which permits termination for failure to effectuate program goals or agency priorities only if such conditions are “clearly and unambiguously” specified in the award terms and “to the extent authorized by law.”

Throughout, the states have emphasized the factual context of a nationwide teacher shortage and the role of multi‑year TQP/SEED awards in recruiting, training, and retaining teachers for hard‑to‑staff subjects and underserved districts.

They cite reliance by programs in their jurisdictions—for example, UMass initiatives to license early childhood and bilingual special‑education teachers, CSU/UC programs addressing rural and special‑education needs, SUNY/CUNY residencies, Montclair State and The College of New Jersey residencies, Milwaukee Public Schools special‑education residencies through UW–Madison, and CU Denver’s rural teacher pipeline—many mid‑grant when the terminations issued.

Judge Myong J. Joun granted a temporary restraining order on March 10, 2025, requiring the Department to immediately restore the pre‑termination status quo for TQP/SEED awards within the plaintiff states, enjoining implementation or reinstatement of the terminations, and directing notice to grantees and staff.
The TRO issued for 14 days and was later extended to April 7, 2025.

On April 4, 2025, the Supreme Court, in a per curiam opinion, stayed the district court’s order pending appeal, construing the TRO—extended and heavily contested—as an appealable preliminary injunction.
As of June 30, 2025, the Department has moved to dismiss for lack of subject‑matter jurisdiction or, alternatively, to transfer the case to the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (28 U.S.C. § 1631).

Remedies sought are declaratory and injunctive relief vacating the Department’s February grant terminations and directive as applied, reinstating awards consistent with statutory authorizations, and barring re‑termination on unlawful grounds.

The amended complaint (filed June 2, 2025) adds Spending Clause and separation‑of‑powers claims and challenges the Department’s February 2025 “Eliminating Discrimination and Fraud in Department Grant Awards” directive, linking it to Executive Orders 14151, 14173, and 14190.

Plaintiffs name the United States, the Secretary of Defense Peter B. Hegseth, the service secretaries and their departments (Army, Navy/Marine Corps, Air Force/Space Force), and the Director and agency of the Defense Health Agency in their official capacities.
The case is before Judge Ana C. Reyes.
Plaintiffs challenge two presidential orders issued at the start of 2025 and the Department of Defense’s implementation.

On January 20, 2025, the Administration issued Executive Order 14168, “Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government,” defining “sex” exclusively by biological classification at conception.

On January 27, 2025, Executive Order 14183, “Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness,” revoked the prior open-service policy (EO 14004), stated that adopting a gender identity inconsistent with birth sex is incompatible with military values (honesty, humility, integrity), directed DoD to end “identification‑based pronoun usage,” prohibited males and females from sharing sex‑segregated facilities, and required revisions to DoD medical standards.
On February 7, 2025, DoD paused new accessions for individuals with a history of gender dysphoria and paused transition‑related medical procedures for service members.

On February 26, 2025, DoD issued “Additional Guidance on Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness,” declaring service by people with a current or past diagnosis of, or “symptoms consistent with,” gender dysphoria incompatible with service; directing the services to identify such members within 30 days and initiate separations within 30 days thereafter; canceling transition‑related surgeries; requiring service in birth sex for purposes of pronouns, housing, facilities, and standards; and creating narrow “waivers” available only to individuals who had never attempted transition, had 36 months of “stability” in their birth sex, and agreed to serve in their birth sex.
A Navy recruiting memo (Jan. 28) halted processing of applicants who identify as transgender, and service‑specific guidance followed.
Plaintiffs alleged concrete harms including canceled surgeries, removal from female barracks and latrines for a basic trainee, blocked accessions and graduations, and adverse duty status changes.

Plaintiffs’ operative pleadings (most recently a Fourth Amended Complaint filed March 24, 2025) assert that these actions violate the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause; they also plead procedural due process and estoppel claims.

Plaintiffs seek declaratory relief and temporary, preliminary, and permanent injunctions restoring the prior open-service policy and barring enforcement of EO 14183, aspects of EO 14168 as applied to the military, and DoD’s implementing directives.

On March 21, DoD issued “Military Department Identification” guidance clarifying that “exhibit symptoms consistent with gender dysphoria” refers to DSM‑5 criteria (marked incongruence with clinically significant distress for at least six months), required annual attestations during the Periodic Health Assessment, mandated non‑deployable status for those identified, and directed separation processing.

On March 26, the district court denied dissolution and a stay pending appeal, finding the new guidance confirmed the policy’s focus on transgender people and did not alter the court’s conclusions; the court stayed its order until March 28 at 7:00 p.m. for possible emergency relief from the D.C. Plaintiffs, including current Army, Navy, Air Force, and Space Force personnel and a basic trainee, and transgender applicants whose enlistments or accessions were halted, allege that the orders define sex exclusively by biological classification, revoke the prior open‑service policy, prohibit identification‑based pronoun usage, prevent males and females from sharing sex‑segregated facilities, and require revisions to medical standards. The DoD paused new accessions for individuals with a history of gender dysphoria on February 7, 2025, and issued additional guidance on February 26 that declared service by people with a current or past diagnosis or symptoms consistent with gender dysphoria incompatible, required identification within 30 days and separation within 30 days, canceled transition‑related surgeries, required service in birth sex for pronouns, housing, facilities, and standards, and created narrow waivers for those never attempted transition, 36 months of stability, and agreement to serve in birth sex. A Navy recruiting memo on January 28 halted processing of applicants who identify as transgender. Plaintiffs claim concrete harms including canceled surgeries, removal from female barracks and latrines for a basic trainee, blocked accessions and graduations, and adverse duty status changes. They assert violations of the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, plead procedural due process and estoppel claims, and seek declaratory relief and temporary, preliminary, and permanent injunctions to restore the prior open‑service policy and bar enforcement of the orders and DoD directives. Judge Ana C. Reyes granted a preliminary injunction on March 18, 2025, enjoining EO 14183, the February 26 implementation, and any other actions issued pursuant to that order, and ordering the government to maintain the pre‑January 27 status quo (the 2021–2024 “Austin” policy permitting open service under DoDI 6130.03 Vols. 1 & 2 and DoDI 1300.28). DoD issued “Military Department Identification” guidance on March 21, clarifying DSM‑5 criteria, requiring annual attestations, mandating non‑deployable status, and directing separation processing. The district court denied dissolution on March 26 and stayed its order until March 28. Plaintiffs filed a targeted TRO on March 24, and the D.C. Circuit stayed the injunction on March 27 pending further order. The procedural history includes motions for preliminary injunction (February 3), a temporary restraining order (February 4), status and scheduling conferences, amending complaints (First, Third), hearings (February 18–19), arguments (March 12), and the court’s administrative stay pending appeal. The case is grounded in the prior Austin policy permitting open service under DoDI 6130.03 Vols. 1 & 2 and DoDI 1300.28, with the policy defining sex biologically and the legal claims involving equal protection and procedural due process.

Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I reviewed the case summary and identified the key factual information that establishes the lawsuit, the executive order, the parties, the injunctions, the Supreme Court stay, the class action certification, and related litigation. These facts form the factual basis of the case.

evidence: On January 21, 2025, two immigrant‑rights organizations and several pregnant mothers filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland (Greenbelt Division) challenging Executive Order 14160, “Protecting the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship.” The order directs federal agencies not to recognize birthright citizenship for persons born in the United States after February 19, 2025, when the mother was either unlawfully present or lawfully but temporarily present and the father was neither a United States citizen nor a lawful permanent resident. The plaintiffs—CASA, Inc.; the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project (ASAP); and five individual mothers (later expanded to include additional mothers and newborns)—sued the President, the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, the Secretary of Homeland Security, the Director of USCIS, the Commissioner of the Social Security Administration, and the United States. They sought declaratory and injunctive relief, alleging that the order violates the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause and 8 U.S.C. § 1401(a). Plaintiffs are represented by nonprofit and public‑interest counsel (including CASA counsel and Georgetown University Law Center’s Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection), and the defendants by the Department of Justice.

On February 5, 2025, Judge Deborah L. Boardman granted a preliminary injunction, finding plaintiffs highly likely to succeed on their claim that the Executive Order contradicts the plain language of the Citizenship Clause and the Supreme Court’s decision in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, and also conflicts with § 1401(a). The court rejected the Government’s threshold arguments (including that 8 U.S.C. § 1503 supplied the exclusive remedy), found irreparable harm to newborns and their families, and entered a nationwide injunction enjoining implementation and enforcement of the order by the State Department, DHS/USCIS, the DOJ, the SSA, and persons in active concert with them.

The Government’s motion to stay the injunction was denied in the district court and by the Fourth Circuit. On June 27, 2025, the Supreme Court granted a partial stay in Trump v. CASA, holding that “universal” injunctions likely exceed federal courts’ equitable authority and narrowing the injunction to protect only the named plaintiffs, while expressly permitting agencies to issue guidance and delaying the order’s § 2 effective date by 30 days. The Court did not address the merits of the Executive Order’s legality, and noted that class actions under Rule 23(b)(2) can supply class‑wide injunctive relief.

Within hours, plaintiffs amended their complaint to proceed as a class action on behalf of children born in the United States after February 19, 2025, and their parents. On July 29, 2025, the Fourth Circuit dismissed the interlocutory appeal and remanded to allow the district court to conform its relief to the Supreme Court’s directions and to promptly resolve the class issues. On August 7, 2025, Judge Boardman certified a Rule 23(b)(2) class defined as: “Any child who has been born or will be born in the United States after February 19, 2025, (1) whose mother was unlawfully present in the United States and whose father was not a United States citizen or lawful permanent resident at the time of said person’s birth, or (2) whose mother’s presence in the United States at the time of said person’s birth was lawful but temporary and whose father was not a United States citizen or lawful permanent resident at the time of said person’s birth.” The court found numerosity easily met; identified a common question of law—whether the Executive Order violates the Citizenship Clause and § 1401(a)—capable of class‑wide resolution; and held that the named parents, acting as next friends for their newborns or future children, were typical and adequate representatives for the children’s claims. The court certified only the children’s claims (not the parents’ independent claims), and then issued a classwide preliminary injunction enjoining enforcement of the Executive Order against the certified class pending resolution on the merits.

Key related litigation included similar district‑court injunctions in Washington v. Trump (W.D. Wash.) and Doe v. Trump (D. Mass.), with the Ninth Circuit affirming and the First Circuit denying a stay; the Supreme Court consolidated the Government’s partial‑stay applications from those cases with this one. Judge Boardman’s principal reported opinions are the February 5, 2025 preliminary‑injunction decision (763 F. Supp. 3d 723) and the February 18, 2025 decision denying a partial stay (2025 WL 545840). The Supreme Court’s partial‑stay ruling is reported at 145 S. Ct. 2540 (2025). No trial has occurred, and the case remains pending on the merits, with a classwide preliminary injunction in place enjoining enforcement of Executive Order 14160 as to all class members.
extracted.value: The case involves a lawsuit filed on January 21, 2025 by CASA, Inc., the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project (ASAP), and five pregnant mothers challenging Executive Order 14160, which restricts birthright citizenship for children born in the United States after February 19, 2025 to mothers who were unlawfully or temporarily present and fathers who are not U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. The plaintiffs alleged violations of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause and 8 U.S.C. § 1401(a). On February 5, 2025, Judge Deborah L. Boardman granted a preliminary injunction enjoining enforcement of the order. The government sought and was denied a stay, and on June 27, 2025, the Supreme Court granted a partial stay, narrowing the injunction to the named plaintiffs and allowing agencies to issue guidance. Plaintiffs amended to a class action, and on August 7, 2025, Judge Boardman certified a Rule 23(b)(2) class of all children born after February 19, 2025 meeting the specified criteria, and issued a classwide preliminary injunction pending resolution on the merits. Related litigation includes Washington v. Trump and Doe v. Trump, with similar injunctions and stays.

evidence: In May 2020, during the COVID‑19 pandemic, two lawsuits challenging Louisiana’s absentee and early voting rules were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana and were later consolidated before Chief Judge Shelly D. Dick.

On May 7, 2020, community organizations and voters (including Power Coalition for Equity and Justice and the Louisiana NAACP) sued the Governor and Secretary of State in Power Coalition for Equity & Justice v. Edwards.

On May 19, 2020, individual voters and two civic groups (Telisa Clark, Lakeshia Barnett, Crescent City Media Group, and the League of Women Voters of Louisiana) filed a related action against the Governor, Secretary of State, the Attorney General, and two parish registrars (Lafayette and Terrebonne).

Plaintiffs brought claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, alleging that, in the context of COVID‑19, three state voting rules unconstitutionally burdened the right to vote and violated the Voting Rights Act: (1) the “Excuse Requirement,” which limits absentee‑by‑mail voting to specific categories in La. Rev. Stat. § 18:1303; (2) the absentee ballot “Witness Requirement,” which requires a witness signature on the absentee ballot certificate (La. Rev. Stat. § 18:1306(E)(2)(a)); and (3) the lack of notice and an opportunity to cure defects in absentee applications or ballots (La. Rev. Stat. § 18:1313).

A revised Emergency Election Plan, approved April 27, 2020, created five COVID‑related excuses for absentee voting for the July 11 and August 15 elections, extended early voting to thirteen days for those elections, but retained the witness requirement and did not cover the November and December elections.
On June 11, 2020, the Governor signed SB 75, immediately limiting any one person (except an immediate family member) from witnessing more than one absentee ballot.

On June 15, 2020, the Secretary, with the Attorney General’s approval, issued an emergency rule allowing limited notice‑and‑cure of absentee ballot deficiencies, but requiring voters to appear in person at the registrar’s office to cure.
On June 22, 2020, the Court dismissed the consolidated cases for lack of subject matter jurisdiction on standing grounds, without reaching the merits or the other defenses.

evidence: On April 22, 2020, several South Carolina voters and a nonprofit (later joined by the South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP) filed this federal civil‑rights action against the Executive Director and members of the South Carolina State Election Commission and the Governor, challenging two absentee‑voting provisions in light of COVID‑19: (1) the “Excuse Requirement” limiting who may vote absentee (S.C. Code Ann. § 7‑15‑320), and (2) the “Witness Requirement” mandating a witness signature on an absentee ballot envelope (S.C. Code Ann. § 7‑15‑380).

Plaintiffs alleged these provisions, during the pandemic, imposed unconstitutional burdens on the right to vote in violation of the First and Fourteenth Amendments (42 U.S.C. § 1983), denied or abridged the right to vote in violation of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, constituted a prohibited “test or device” under Section 201 of the Voting Rights Act, and violated Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

Plaintiffs supported their claims with public‑health guidance from CDC and DHEC, evidence that many voters—disproportionately Black, elderly, or disabled—live alone or must strictly quarantine, and a March 30, 2020 letter from Executive Director Marci Andino to state leaders recommending, for safety and security, temporary no‑excuse absentee voting and removal of the witness requirement.

On May 25, 2020, Judge J. Michelle Childs granted in part plaintiffs’ motion for a preliminary injunction, enjoining enforcement of the Witness Requirement for the June 9, 2020 primaries and any runoffs.

The court found that, amid COVID‑19, requiring a witness signature forced voters—especially those living alone or at high risk—to risk exposure to vote, constituting a severe burden on the right to vote that was not justified by the State’s asserted interests, particularly given other safeguards and the SEC Director’s acknowledgment that the witness signature “offers no benefit” to election officials.
On September 16, 2020, the General Assembly enacted H.B. 5305 (R.149), suspending the Excuse Requirement for the November general election due to the ongoing emergency.
On September 18, 2020, in a related case (Middleton v. Andino), the same court enjoined the Witness Requirement for the November 2020 general election.

In light of those developments, Judge Childs stayed the Thomas proceedings and held all pending motions in abeyance, noting both challenged provisions were suspended or enjoined for November 2020. The case remains stayed.

The South Carolina Republican Party intervened (permissively) to defend the challenged provisions, and the Attorney General (amicus) and United States (Statement of Interest) opposed the Section 201 “test or device” claim, noting such claims must be heard by a three‑judge court and arguing a witness signature is not a prohibited voucher.
Protection & Advocacy for People with Disabilities filed an amicus brief supporting plaintiffs. Later, the Speaker of the House and the Senate President were also allowed to intervene.

After the General Assembly enacted S. 635 (Act 133) on May 13, 2020 temporarily allowing all qualified voters to vote absentee in the June primaries due to the state of emergency, the Excuse Requirement issue for those elections became moot.

Plaintiffs filed an amended complaint on July 13, 2020 seeking relief for the remaining 2020 elections. Defendants moved for summary judgment on August 10, 2020, arguing lack of standing, that absentee voting is a privilege subject to rational‑basis review under McDonald v. Board of Election Comm’rs, that the burdens were minimal given in‑person safety measures, and that neither the VRA nor ADA claims could succeed.

evidence: On April 21, 2020, pretrial detainees and a post‑conviction inmate at the Prince George’s County Correctional Center filed a class action in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland (Judge Paula Xinis), alleging unconstitutional jail conditions during the COVID‑19 pandemic.

Plaintiffs—represented by Civil Rights Corps and WilmerHale—seek declaratory and injunctive relief under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for violations of the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments, and habeas relief under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 for a subclass of medically vulnerable pretrial detainees.

They ask the court to remedy unsafe conditions (lack of no‑cost soap and sanitizer, poor sanitation, inadequate masking and social distancing), delays and co‑pays for medical care (including $4 sick‑call fees), failure to medically isolate and contact trace, and filthy medical isolation cells with minimal monitoring or access to hygiene.
Plaintiffs also allege a policy of “overdetention” of detainees who had satisfied their release but were held solely due to COVID‑19 positivity until deemed non‑contagious.

The court found Plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits of their Eighth and Fourteenth Amendment conditions claims based on a “triple‑threat” at the Facility: undertesting (including early test positivity of 90%), inadequate treatment and isolation of symptomatic detainees, and no plan to protect high‑risk detainees.

Defendant filed the required plans and reports. On May 26, 2020, the Facility outlined processes to identify high‑risk detainees (via Chronic Care Clinic lists, intake, and sick‑call screening), monitor and treat them, house them (favoring single‑celling where possible), and to continue training and testing. In a June 5, 2020 14‑day report, Defendant stated that by May 26, 2020, 521 of 525 detainees had been tested, with six asymptomatic positives (about 1.14%); new intakes were being tested and quarantined for 14 days.

On July 7, 2020, Plaintiffs filed a First Amended Complaint adding two claims challenging the jail’s prolonged, universal lockdown (confinement in cells for 22–23 hours per day with limited out‑of‑cell time often in the middle of the night, scarce reading materials, and curtailed mental health services).
The court observed substantial evidence that the jail’s grievance process was “hobbled, if not outright broken,” bearing on PLRA exhaustion.

Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I identified the key facts in the summary: the filing date and parties, the allegations of ICE's COVID‑19 response violating due process and the Accardi doctrine, the court orders, the Special Master report, and the settlement. These facts form the factual basis. I extracted the relevant excerpts and compiled them as evidence.

evidence: On April 13, 2020, civil immigration detainees held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at three South Florida facilities—Krome Service Processing Center (Miami), Broward Transitional Center (Pompano Beach), and Glades County Detention Center (Moore Haven)—filed a class action habeas and injunctive suit (28 U.S.C. § 2241) against the ICE Miami Field Office Director and the U.S. Attorney General.

Represented by a coalition of private counsel (King & Spalding and others), nonprofit legal organizations (Americans for Immigrant Justice, Southern Poverty Law Center, Legal Aid Service of Broward County), and the University of Miami School of Law Immigration Clinic, the detainees alleged that ICE’s response to COVID‑19 at the facilities violated the Fifth Amendment due process right to reasonably safe, non‑punitive civil detention and, under the Accardi doctrine, ICE’s own binding detention standards requiring compliance with Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidance.

They sought declaratory and injunctive relief, including release, to address the risk of infection, the use of cohort quarantine contrary to CDC guidance, inadequate access to masks, soap, and disinfectants, and unsafe transfers that allegedly spread infection.

After expedited proceedings before U.S. Magistrate Judge Jonathan Goodman, District Judge Marcia G. Cooke entered a Temporary Restraining Order on April 30, 2020, requiring ICE to: (1) evaluate each named petitioner for release and report who could be promptly released; (2) describe how it would accelerate review and reduce each facility to roughly 75% of capacity within two weeks; (3) file weekly and twice‑weekly reports on releases and facility populations (including “mandatory detainees” and those with no convictions or pending charges); (4) immediately provide detainees with adequate soap, water, cleaning materials, and weekly mask replacement; and (5) provide staff and detainee education on COVID‑19.

On May 2, 2020, the Court clarified that transfers were permitted only after ICE evaluated each detainee’s eligibility for release pursuant to ICE’s April 10, 2020 COVID‑19 Pandemic Response Requirements (PRR).

Following evidentiary hearings on June 2–3, 2020, Judge Cooke issued an Omnibus Order on June 6, 2020, granting a preliminary injunction, finding record evidence that ICE failed to protect detainees from COVID‑19 and had not adhered to CDC and ICE standards, and certifying a Rule 23(b)(2) class of “all current civil immigration detainees who are held by ICE at Krome, BTC, and Glades when this action was filed, since this action was filed, or in the future.”

The Court ordered ICE to stop commingling confirmed COVID‑19 cases with unconfirmed cases; provide unrestricted access to hand soap, hand sanitizer, and hand towels; provide masks and COVID‑19 education to all detainees and staff; and perform CDC‑compliant screening before any detainee transfer.

Disputes over compliance led to Petitioners’ motion to compel. On July 17, 2020, the Court appointed Special Master Matthew C. Dates to inspect the facilities and report on compliance with the preliminary injunction.

The Special Master’s February 19, 2021 report found, among other things, that cleaning supplies, masks, soap, and sanitizer were available and logged, but that the facilities’ physical layouts impeded full social distancing; he recommended partial relief.
On March 25, 2021, the Court granted in part and denied in part Petitioners’ motion to compel, adopting aspects of the Special Master’s findings and continuing enforcement of the injunction.
On June 28, 2021, the parties entered a class‑wide Settlement Agreement, adopted as a final, court‑enforceable injunction with the Court retaining jurisdiction.

The settlement requires the three facilities to comply with applicable detention standards, the ICE PRR, and CDC guidelines as they evolve; to implement ICE’s COVID‑19 Vaccination Guidelines and Protocol and provide free COVID‑19 vaccinations (and seasonal influenza vaccines), with multilingual educational materials and medical staff presentations; and to provide vaccine cards and information to those released after one vaccine dose.

The facilities must maintain population density in each living area and overall at no more than 75% of capacity (as defined by PRR/CDC) with limited, reportable exceptions; post daily cohort/quarantine status and dates in every housing unit; test symptomatic detainees and close contacts within 24 hours and provide results within 12 hours; isolate positives and medically isolate exposed, test‑negative detainees for 14 days without mixing with confirmed cases; medically isolate those pending test results away from general population; and ensure unlimited, no‑cost access to soap and hand sanitizer with logged refills at specified locations.

The facilities must provide new masks (disposable masks three times per week or clean cloth masks) with immediate replacement on request; require staff to wear masks; provide a new mask before any transfer; and perform a rapid COVID‑19 test within 24 hours before transfer, only transferring those who test negative.
Transport vehicles must be sanitized before and after each trip and seat detainees with distancing when possible.
Class members retain the right to pursue individual habeas petitions for release.
Throughout, Judge Marcia G. Cooke presided, with Magistrate Judge Jonathan Goodman handling emergency and class certification proceedings, and Special Master Dates monitoring compliance.
The case concluded with a court‑enforced settlement aimed at aligning facility practices with CDC and ICE standards to mitigate COVID‑19 risks for the certified class.
extracted.value: The case involves civil immigration detainees at Krome Service Processing Center, Broward Transitional Center, and Glades County Detention Center who filed a class action on April 13, 2020 alleging ICE’s COVID‑19 response violated due process and the Accardi doctrine, citing inadequate masks, soap, disinfectants, cohort quarantine contrary to CDC guidance, and unsafe transfers that spread infection. The allegations are supported by a Temporary Restraining Order issued on April 30, 2020, a preliminary injunction on June 6, 2020, and a Special Master report in February 2021 confirming ICE’s non‑compliance. Background information includes ICE’s April 10, 2020 COVID‑19 Pandemic Response Requirements and CDC guidelines. The parties settled on June 28, 2021, agreeing that the facilities must comply with ICE’s PRR, CDC guidelines, and provide vaccinations, unlimited hygiene supplies, mask protocols, and other health safeguards, with the court retaining jurisdiction.

The facilities must maintain population density in each living area and overall at no more than 75% of capacity (as defined by PRR/CDC) with limited, reportable exceptions; post daily cohort/quarantine status and dates in every housing unit; test symptomatic detainees and close contacts within 24 hours and provide results within 12 hours; isolate positives and medically isolate exposed, test‑negative detainees for 14 days without mixing with confirmed cases; medically isolate those pending test results away from general population; and ensure unlimited, no‑cost access to soap and hand sanitizer with logged refills at specified locations. The facilities must provide new masks (disposable masks three times per week or clean cloth masks) with immediate replacement on request; require staff to wear masks; provide a new mask before any transfer; and perform a rapid COVID‑19 test within 24 hours before transfer, only transferring those who test negative. Transport vehicles must be sanitized before and after each trip and seat detainees with distancing when possible. Class members retain the right to pursue individual habeas petitions for release.
